problemText: A satellite image is a picture of the ground taken from which location?
choices: From a camera on a satellite far out in space above Earth
From a camera in an aircraft flying close to the ground
From a drawing made by a mapmaker sitting at a desk
From a camera on the ground pointing upward at the sky
hints: The name 'satellite image' gives you a clue about where the camera is located.
This picture is taken from much higher up than an aerial photograph.

problemText: A mapmaker draws a map of a city park. The mapmaker labels the park's name, the walking paths, and the benches. At the exact same time, a photographer in an airplane takes an aerial view of the same park and captures the grass, trees, paths, benches, and a person sleeping on one of the benches. Which feature appears in the aerial view but is least likely to appear on the mapmaker's map?
choices: The walking paths, because they are drawn features that mapmakers always include
The person sleeping on the bench, because the mapmaker did not plan for anyone to be there at that moment
The park's name, because it is a label made of letters and words rather than a physical object on the ground
The trees, because they change size and shape throughout the year depending on the season
hints: Remember that a picture records whatever is physically present at that exact moment, whether or not it was planned for.
A map shows only what a mapmaker chose to draw ahead of time.

problemText: A student looks at a satellite image of a coast and sees where the land ends and the ocean begins. She then looks at a map of the same coast. On the map, she sees a line marking where one country's territory ends and another country's territory begins, drawn right along the coast. Why does the satellite image show the land-and-ocean edge but the map must draw the country boundary line?
choices: Because satellite images can only record natural features that reflect light, while maps are tools designed by people to represent human decisions like where boundaries should be drawn
Because the satellite image was taken from a camera that is programmed to ignore boundary lines, whereas mapmakers are trained to draw every single line they see on the ground
Because the land and ocean are real physical features that appear in pictures, while a country boundary is a line a person drew on a map to show a choice
Because satellites are positioned too high in space to detect thin painted lines on the ground, so mapmakers must add boundary lines that cannot be seen from orbit
hints: Think about what is actually painted or marked on the ground itself.
One of these lines is a real physical feature; the other exists only because someone decided to draw it.

problemText: A city builds a new road last month. Today, a satellite image of the city is taken, and a cartographer finishes drawing an updated map of the city. The satellite image clearly shows the new road as a paved surface, but the cartographer's new map does not include the road. Which two reasons together best explain why the new road appears in one but not the other?
choices: The road is made of dark asphalt that satellites can easily photograph, but the cartographer used an old map that was drawn before the road was built
Satellite images can only show new roads, while maps can only show old roads, so the two tools show completely different things
The satellite camera captured the road because it took the picture on a sunny day, but the cartographer's map was incomplete because it rained while she was drawing it
The satellite image records whatever physical feature exists at that moment, but the map only shows features the mapmaker chose to draw, and the mapmaker may not have known about the new road yet
hints: A picture captures whatever is actually there on the ground right now; a map reflects what a person decided to include.
The mapmaker may have completed the map before finding out about the new road, or may have chosen not to include it.

problemText: A student claims that an aerial view is exactly the same thing as a satellite image, just with a different name, and that therefore a satellite image can show everything a map can show. Which part of this claim is wrong, and why?
choices: Both parts are wrong; the two pictures are taken from different heights, and neither picture can show a boundary line that has no physical mark on the ground
Only the second part is wrong; satellite images and aerial views are truly the same tool, but no picture can show a boundary line with no physical mark on the ground
Only the first part is wrong; aerial views and satellite images are taken from different heights, but both pictures can show invisible boundary lines that maps can draw
Neither part is wrong; they describe the same tool, and that tool can indeed show everything a map shows, only better
hints: Check what makes a satellite image different from an aerial view in terms of where the camera is located.
Then check whether any picture, no matter how clear, can capture a line that is not physically painted or marked on the ground.

problemText: A nature preserve has a stream running through it. The stream flows out of the preserve and into a river that forms the boundary between two states. A satellite image taken today shows the stream clearly and the river's path, but shows no line separating one state from the other. A map of the preserve shows the stream, the river, the state boundary as a thick line, and the name of each state. How is it possible for the map to show something the satellite image cannot show, and yet the satellite image shows something a blank map could easily miss?
choices: The satellite image was taken from high altitude which allowed it to see flowing water like streams and rivers, but the altitude was too great to detect the thin line that marks a state boundary on the ground
The map shows the state boundary line because a mapmaker drew it, but the satellite image shows the stream's current shape because it is a picture of what is really there right now
The satellite can photograph only features made of solid material, so it captures streams and rivers but cannot capture abstract boundaries that exist only in law and agreement between states

The satellite image cannot show state boundaries because the boundary line is invisible on the ground itself, existing only in legal documents and on maps, whereas the stream is a physical water feature that reflects light
hints: A boundary line between two states is usually not painted on the ground, but a stream is a real physical feature.
Think about what each tool does best: one captures what is actually there at that moment, and the other can label and add lines that a person chooses to draw.

problemText: A bar graph shows the population of four towns. A longer bar on this graph represents what?
choices: A bigger area of land
A town that is farther away
A town that is older
A bigger number of people
hints: Think about what a bar graph is designed to show—the definition tells you exactly what the bar's length means.
A longer bar always stands for a bigger number in the data.

problemText: A pie chart shows how a city's 100 square kilometers of land is used for different purposes. Forests cover 35 percent of the pie chart. How many square kilometers of the city's land is covered by forests?
choices: 35 square kilometers
65 square kilometers
100 square kilometers
135 square kilometers
hints: Remember that a percent is a share of the whole. Here, the whole is 100 square kilometers.
When the whole is 100 of something, the percent number and the actual amount are the same.

problemText: A table shows rainfall amounts in three months for a city: March, 40 millimeters. April, 55 millimeters. May, 30 millimeters. How much more rainfall did April receive than May?
choices: 15 millimeters
25 millimeters
85 millimeters
95 millimeters
hints: Find the two numbers you need to compare from the table—one for April and one for May.
Subtract the smaller amount from the larger amount, and keep the unit with your answer.

problemText: A bar graph shows annual snowfall in four regions: North, 80 centimeters. South, 20 centimeters. East, 35 centimeters. West, 45 centimeters. Which two regions together received more snowfall than the other two regions combined? By how many centimeters?
choices: North and East together; 20 more centimeters
South and East together; 30 more centimeters
North and West together; 40 more centimeters
East and West together; 10 more centimeters
hints: You need to test different pairs by adding them up. Don't assume the biggest single bar is automatically part of the winning pair.
Add all four regions' totals first to check your work: the two pair totals must add up to that year total.

problemText: Two countries' pie charts show their forest coverage. Country A's pie chart shows Forests at 60 percent of A's total land area of 50 square kilometers. Country B's pie chart shows Forests at 80 percent of B's total land area of 30 square kilometers. Which country has more actual forest area in square kilometers?
choices: Country A, because 60 percent is less than 80 percent
Country B, because 80 percent is more than 60 percent
They have the same forest area because both percents are less than 100 percent
Country A, because 60 percent of 50 equals 30 square kilometers
hints: A bigger percent in one pie chart does not automatically mean a bigger amount, because the two countries' wholes may be different sizes.
Calculate the actual forest area for each country by multiplying the percent times the total land area, then compare those two amounts.

problemText: A table shows the number of endangered bird species in five regions: Region 1, 8 species. Region 2, 12 species. Region 3, 5 species. Region 4, 9 species. Region 5, 6 species. A student claims that Region 2 alone has more endangered birds than Regions 3 and 4 combined. Is the student correct? Which statement best explains why or why not?
choices: No, the student is incorrect; Regions 3 and 4 together have 14 species, which is more than Region 2's 12 species
Yes, the student is correct, because Region 2's bar would be taller than any other single bar on a bar graph
Yes, the student is correct; 12 is more than 5, so Region 2 has more species than Region 3
No, the student is incorrect; the three regions are too far apart in the table to be compared accurately
hints: A comparison question always needs two numbers read correctly and then compared. Find both numbers from the table.
Never stop at reading a single bar or region—you must add the regions you are comparing together before you can say whether the claim is true or false.

problemText: A GPS receiver picks up a radio signal sent out by a satellite. What is the one piece of information that this signal allows the receiver to figure out?
choices: The exact location where the receiver is standing
How far away the satellite is from the receiver
Whether the satellite is moving toward or away from the receiver
The name and identification number of the satellite
hints: Think about what a single distance tells you — is it enough by itself to pinpoint one exact spot, or does it only narrow the search?
Each satellite signal gives the receiver one piece of information to work with. What is that one thing?

problemText: A car's GPS receiver picks up a signal from one satellite and calculates that it is exactly 15,000 miles away from that satellite. Based on this distance alone, how many different locations on Earth could the car be parked at?
choices: Exactly one location, because the satellite can only be in one place at a time
Exactly two locations, because circles intersect at two points in space
Many different locations — all points that are 15,000 miles away from the satellite
All locations within 15,000 miles of the satellite, forming a sphere around it
hints: Imagine drawing a circle around a satellite. Every point on that circle is the same distance from the center. Now think about whether the car must be on that circle or inside it.
One distance from one satellite narrows the search area from the whole Earth down to what shape?

problemText: A student claims: 'If a GPS receiver gets a very strong, very clear signal from one satellite, the receiver can figure out its exact location right away.' Is this student correct? Why or why not?
choices: Yes, because a strong signal gives the receiver enough electrical power to process location data without needing additional satellites for triangulation
No, because the receiver does not have permission to receive signals from satellites and must wait for authorization from ground control
Yes, because the satellite sends back encoded location information through the strength of the signal itself, allowing the receiver to decode its position
No, because signal strength and signal count are different; one satellite's distance, no matter how clear, still creates a circle of possible spots, not one exact point
hints: Does a strong, clear signal give you more satellites to work with, or just a clearer read on the one satellite you already have?
Remember: one distance makes a circle, not a point. Can signal strength change that?

problemText: A GPS receiver picks up signals from Satellite A and Satellite B, works out its distance from each one, and draws two circles on a map — one around Satellite A and one around Satellite B. These two circles cross at exactly two points on the map. The receiver's true location is at one of these two points, but it cannot yet tell which one. What must happen next for the receiver to narrow the search down to one exact spot?
choices: Pick up a signal from a third satellite, work out the distance to it, and see which of the two points also lies on that third circle
Combine the two existing distances again, using a mathematical formula that factors in Earth's curvature to eliminate one of the intersection points
Ask the satellites to send a stronger confirmation signal that identifies which point matches the receiver's actual ground elevation and altitude
Wait for Satellite A or Satellite B to move to a new orbital position so their circles no longer overlap at two locations
hints: You have two circles and two crossing points. What you need is something to distinguish between them — what geometric object would that be?
Two distances gave you two points. What does a third distance add to the picture?

problemText: A hiker stands on a mountain and her GPS receiver picks up signals from Satellites P, Q, and R. The receiver calculates distances of 20,000 km from P, 22,000 km from Q, and 21,000 km from R. The receiver combines all three of these distances and identifies one exact spot on the map as the hiker's location. Which of the following statements is true about this result?
choices: The satellite that sent the strongest signal determined the final location
All three distances together narrow the search down to one spot, and that spot matches all three distances equally
Only one of the three distances actually matters; the other two are just backup
The receiver had to ignore one of the distances because the three circles did not all cross at the same point
hints: Think about what it means for a point to be the correct location: does it have to match just one distance, or all of them?
The receiver combines the distances from several satellites. What would confirm that a single spot is the right answer?

problemText: A satellite in space sends the same radio signal out to anyone in range — whether or not any receiver is listening, and whether or not the satellite knows a receiver is there. A farmer with a GPS receiver is standing on the ground in a field, far away from any ground control station. The farmer's receiver picks up that satellite's signal, works out a distance from it, and eventually pinpoints the farmer's exact location. In this scenario, who or what device actually figured out where the farmer was standing, and why did the figuring-out happen on that device rather than on the satellite?
choices: The satellite figured it out by using signals sent back from the farmer's receiver to calculate distance and location accurately
Both the satellite and the receiver figured it out together, because they need to be in constant two-way contact to exchange calculations
The farmer's GPS receiver figured it out by listening to signals and doing calculations, because the satellite has no way to know the receiver exists or where it is
The ground control station figured it out by combining signals from all satellites and receivers, because individual receivers lack the power to perform such complex calculations
hints: A GPS receiver only listens — it does not send anything back up to the satellite. If it does not send anything, what does that tell you about whether the satellite can know the receiver's location?
Where does all the calculation work happen — inside the satellite, or inside the device on the ground?

problemText: A thematic map uses a key to show what each color or symbol on the map means. Before you answer any question about a thematic map, what should you do first?
choices: Look at which color or symbol appears most often on the map
Find the area the question asks about and then look for its color or symbol
Read every entry in the key from top to bottom before looking at any area on the map
Search the key for only the color or symbol the question mentions
hints: The first step with any thematic map is to install one habit before doing anything else.
You need to know what every single entry means before you try to match any area to the key.

problemText: A thematic map of the country of Ravenbay shows tree cover using three shades of green. The key states: light green means sparse tree cover, medium green means moderate tree cover, and dark green means dense tree cover. According to the map description, Hilltop is shaded medium green and Lakeside is shaded dark green. Which statement is correct?
choices: Hilltop has denser tree cover than Lakeside because it is listed first in the problem description
Hilltop has more tree cover because medium green represents a deeper shade of green than light green does
Both regions have the same amount of tree cover since they are both shown using shades of the same color
Lakeside has denser tree cover than Hilltop because the key lists dark green as dense tree cover
hints: Match each region's shade to the key entry, then compare what the key says about each shade.
The key is the source of meaning—look up what dark green stands for and what medium green stands for.

problemText: A thematic map of the region of Westmarch shows different types of land use. The key uses symbols: a pine tree symbol for forest, a crossed pickaxe symbol for mining, and a factory symbol for industrial zones. On the map, Northpeak is marked with a pine tree symbol and Deepvale is marked with a crossed pickaxe symbol. A student claims that Northpeak has industrial zones because it is located at the top of the map. What is wrong with this student's reasoning?
choices: The student looked at the position of the area on the map instead of reading the key and matching the symbol
The student relied on compass direction rather than using the map scale to calculate distance from industrial areas
The student interpreted the pine tree symbol as representing both forest and industrial use, which are not the same thing
The student assumed that areas drawn with larger symbols on the map represent industrial zones rather than checking the key
hints: A symbol key tells you the meaning of each symbol—position on the map does not change what a symbol means.
To answer correctly, you must match the symbol to the key, not guess based on where the area sits.

problemText: A thematic map of the territory of Silverpine shows annual snowfall using three shades of gray. The key states: light gray means low snowfall, medium gray means moderate snowfall, and dark gray means heavy snowfall. On the map, Northridge is shaded dark gray, Midvalley is shaded medium gray, Southplain is shaded light gray, and Westbrook is shaded dark gray. A question asks: 'Which regions receive moderate snowfall according to the key?' If the same map were used to answer a different question about which regions have the most forests, would the snowfall key still answer that question?
choices: Yes, because the key shows three different shades and three different regions can be compared
No, because the key is built to show snowfall data only, and forest cover is a different topic
Yes, because darker shades always mean larger or more important amounts on any map
No, because the key is printed in gray and forests are typically green
hints: A thematic map is designed around one chosen topic—ask yourself what topic this key is built to show.
A key built to show one kind of data cannot answer a question about a completely different kind of data.

problemText: A thematic map of the state of Timberbrook shows the main economic activity in each county using symbols: a wheat bundle means agriculture, a gear means manufacturing, and a dollar sign means services. On the map, Clearfield is marked with a wheat bundle, Ridgeton is marked with a gear, Millbrook is marked with a dollar sign, and Ashford is marked with a wheat bundle. A student looks at the map and says, 'The gear symbol looks more detailed and complex than the wheat symbol, so manufacturing must be more important than agriculture in Timberbrook.' Explain what is wrong with this reasoning and state which counties have agriculture as their main activity according to the key.
choices: The student should have counted how many times each symbol appears on the map and concluded that the most frequently appearing symbol represents the most important activity in Timberbrook
The student is correct that the gear symbol looks more complex in design, but agriculture is still more important because wheat is the traditional crop; only Clearfield shows agriculture
In a symbol key, each symbol is a separate category with no ranking, so the look or size of a symbol says nothing about importance; Clearfield and Ashford have agriculture as their main activity
In a symbol key, symbols that appear darker or bolder represent more important industries in a region; only Ashford displays agriculture because it is the last county mentioned
hints: In a symbol key, no symbol is naturally bigger, bolder, or more important than another—only the key's stated meaning matters.
To find all counties with agriculture, read the key to see which symbol stands for agriculture, then find every area marked with that same symbol on the map.

problemText: A thematic map of the nation of Crowland shows two kinds of information: a shaded key using colors to represent population density (light yellow for low, medium orange for medium, dark red for high), and a symbol key using marks to show the main industry (a wheat symbol for farming, a gear symbol for manufacturing, a fish symbol for fishing). The map shows four regions: Northen is shaded medium orange with a fish symbol, Eastmarch is shaded dark red with a gear symbol, Westfield is shaded light yellow with a wheat symbol, and Southwick is shaded dark red with a wheat symbol. A student is asked: 'Which regions have both high population density AND farming as the main industry?' The student answers 'Eastmarch, because it is shaded dark red, which the key lists as high population density.' Explain what is wrong with the student's answer, identify the correct answer, and state why the student made this error.
choices: The student read the color key correctly but the symbol key is printed upside down; the correct answer is Westfield, because it appears last on the map
The student looked at the wrong map and confused the location; the correct answer is Eastmarch and Southwick, because both are shaded dark red
The student forgot to read the entire key; the correct answer is Northen, because it has the most symbols on the map

The student matched only the color to the key and ignored the symbol key; the correct answer is Southwick, because it is shaded dark red (high population density) AND marked with a wheat symbol (farming)
hints: This question requires you to match data from TWO different keys—one for population density and one for industry—before combining them.
The student found one piece of correct information (high population density) but forgot to check the symbol key for the second piece (farming as main industry).
